docs.title: pyramids-citymodels
docs.text: Reads and writes the file formats of semantic 3D city models — CityGML, CityJSON and more — as pyramids objects. pyramids-core already ships the GIS data model and the operations that follow once features are in hand; what it does not do is open the city-model exchange formats. That is this package's only job.

docs.title: The layer boundary
docs.text:
The split is the point of the package, so it is worth stating precisely. pyramids-core owns the GIS data model and everything that follows from features already in hand:

Concern Lives in The raster Dataset, the vector FeatureCollection, the datacube pyramids GDAL/OGR-backed read / write of the formats GDAL already handles pyramids Reprojection, overlays, spatial joins, filtering, geometry predicates pyramids Vector ↔ raster conversion, feature extraction, spatial indexing pyramids

pyramids-citymodels adds the one thing that is missing from that list — the ability to open 3D city-model exchange formats:

Concern Lives in Reading CityGML, CityJSON, and related interchange formats pyramids_citymodels.drivers Writing the formats that support a faithful round-trip pyramids_citymodels.drivers Driver discovery via the pyramids.vector_drivers entry points pyramids-core reads, this package registers

Anything that belongs on the left-hand side of the first table is a change to pyramids-core, not a feature of this package. Report it upstream rather than duplicating it here.

docs.title: Status
docs.text:
0.1.0 is the repository scaffold — packaging, CI, docs, and the import contract that pins import pyramids first so the vendored osgeo bindings are active before anything else loads. The public surface is empty; pyramids_citymodels.__version__ is all it exports.

>>> import pyramids_citymodels
>>> pyramids_citymodels.__version__
'0.1.0'

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
A primary goal of pyramids-citymodels is to be inclusive to the largest number of contributors, with the most varied and diverse backgrounds possible. As such, we are committed to providing a friendly, safe and welcoming environment for all, regardless of gender, sexual orientation, ability, ethnicity, socioeconomic status, and religion (or lack thereof).

This code of conduct outlines our expectations for all those who participate in our community, as well as the consequences for unacceptable behavior.

We invite all those who participate in pyramids-citymodels to help us create safe and positive experiences for everyone.

docs.title: 2. Open [Source/Culture/Tech] Citizenship
docs.text:
A supplemental goal of this Code of Conduct is to increase open [source/culture/tech] citizenship by encouraging participants to recognize and strengthen the relationships between our actions and their effects on our community.

Communities mirror the societies in which they exist and positive action is essential to counteract the many forms of inequality and abuses of power that exist in society.

If you see someone who is making an extra effort to ensure our community is welcoming, friendly, and encourages all participants to contribute to the fullest extent, we want to know.

docs.title: 3. Expected Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are expected and requested of all community members:

  • Participate in an authentic and active way. In doing so, you contribute to the health and longevity of this community.
  • Exercise consideration and respect in your speech and actions.
  • Attempt collaboration before conflict.
  • Refrain from demeaning, discriminatory, or harassing behavior and speech.
  • Be mindful of your surroundings and of your fellow participants. Alert community leaders if you notice a dangerous situation, someone in distress, or violations of this Code of Conduct, even if they seem inconsequential.
  • Remember that community event venues may be shared with members of the public; please be respectful to all patrons of these locations.

docs.title: 4. Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
The following behaviors are considered harassment and are unacceptable within our community:

  • Violence, threats of violence or violent language directed against another person.
  • Sexist, racist, homophobic, transphobic, ableist or otherwise discriminatory jokes and language.
  • Posting or displaying sexually explicit or violent material.
  • Posting or threatening to post other people's personally identifying information ("doxing").
  • Personal insults, particularly those related to gender, sexual orientation, race, religion, or disability.
  • Inappropriate photography or recording.
  • Inappropriate physical contact. You should have someone's consent before touching them.
  • Unwelcome sexual attention. This includes, sexualized comments or jokes; inappropriate touching, groping, and unwelcomed sexual advances.
  • Deliberate intimidation, stalking or following (online or in person).
  • Advocating for, or encouraging, any of the above behavior.
  • Sustained disruption of community events, including talks and presentations.

docs.title: 5. Weapons Policy
docs.text: No weapons will be allowed at pyramids-citymodels events, community spaces, or in other spaces covered by the scope of this Code of Conduct. Weapons include but are not limited to guns, explosives (including fireworks), and large knives such as those used for hunting or display, as well as any other item used for the purpose of causing injury or harm to others. Anyone seen in possession of one of these items will be asked to leave immediately, and will only be allowed to return without the weapon. Community members are further expected to comply with all state and local laws on this matter.

docs.title: 6. Consequences of Unacceptable Behavior
docs.text:
Unacceptable behavior from any community member, including sponsors and those with decision-making authority, will not be tolerated.

Anyone asked to stop unacceptable behavior is expected to comply immediately.

If a community member engages in unacceptable behavior, the community organizers may take any action they deem appropriate, up to and including a temporary ban or permanent expulsion from the community without warning (and without refund in the case of a paid event).

docs.title: 7. Reporting Guidelines
docs.text:
If you are subject to or witness unacceptable behavior, or have any other concerns, please notify a community organizer as soon as possible. .

Additionally, community organizers are available to help community members engage with local law enforcement or to otherwise help those experiencing unacceptable behavior feel safe. In the context of in-person events, organizers will also provide escorts as desired by the person experiencing distress.

docs.title: 8. Addressing Grievances
docs.text: If you feel you have been falsely or unfairly accused of violating this Code of Conduct, you should notify with a concise description of your grievance. Your grievance will be handled in accordance with our existing governing policies.

docs.title: 9. Scope
docs.text:
We expect all community participants (contributors, paid or otherwise; sponsors; and other guests) to abide by this Code of Conduct in all community venues--online and in-person--as well as in all one-on-one communications pertaining to community business.

This code of conduct and its related procedures also applies to unacceptable behavior occurring outside the scope of community activities when such behavior has the potential to adversely affect the safety and well-being of community members.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
This page covers installation of pyramids-citymodels and its native dependencies.

Item Value Distribution name pyramids-citymodels Python import name pyramids_citymodels Current version 0.1.0 Supported Python 3.11 – 3.14 License GPL v3

Not published yet. 0.1.0 exists only in this repository — there is no PyPI or conda-forge release to install from. Use the from-source route below.

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
• pyramids-core >= 0.70.0 (provides the pyramids import and the city-model driver registry; pulled from PyPI)
  • numpy >= 2.0.0

GDAL is deliberately absent from that list. It is not a dependency of this package: the pyramids-core wheel vendors its own osgeo bindings, and import pyramids is what puts them on sys.path. Nothing here installs or pins a separate GDAL. Several city-model formats (CityGML in particular) are read through GDAL's own drivers, so that vendored osgeo is exactly what these drivers build on.

shapely and geopandas are not declared either. The vector subsystem a city-model driver hands its features to requires them, so they arrive with pyramids-core — but that is its requirement, not a promise to this package. Each gets declared here the moment a module under src/pyramids_citymodels/ imports it directly.

docs.title: Optional extras
docs.text: None yet. One extra per dependency-backed driver family is added when the driver that needs it lands; a bare install stays small, and a driver whose extra is absent is skipped at discovery.

docs.title: Development dependency groups
docs.text:
dev, docs and notebook are PEP 735 dependency groups, not extras — they are local tooling and are deliberately not published in the package metadata. Pixi resolves a group by name wherever an environment lists it: dev is py314 + dev, docs is py314 + docs. notebook is currently referenced by no environment.

pixi install -e dev      # tests, linting, build tooling
pixi install -e docs     # mkdocs toolchain

docs.title: Recommended: Pixi
docs.text:
This repository ships a Pixi configuration that resolves every dependency from PyPI, GDAL included — the pyramids-core wheel vendors its own, so no conda channel is involved and the usual GDAL-wheel headaches do not arise.

Prerequisites: install Pixi.

git clone https://github.com/serapeum-org/pyramids-citymodels.git
cd pyramids-citymodels

# Solve and install the dev environment
pixi install -e dev

# Drop into a shell with everything available
pixi shell -e dev

# Or run a task directly
pixi run main          # main test suite
pixi run test-all      # everything, with a terminal coverage report
pixi run notebooks     # validate example notebooks

Environment Features Purpose default py314 minimal runtime dev py314, dev tests, linting, build tooling docs py314, docs docs site (mkdocs serve) py311 py311, dev pinned Python 3.11 py312 py312, dev pinned Python 3.12 py313 py313, dev pinned Python 3.13 py314 py314, dev pinned Python 3.14

docs.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
docs.text:
This section collects significant architectural decisions for the pyramids-citymodels project, using the MADR format.

  • ADR-0001: Documentation stack
  • ADR-0002: Type checking approach
  • ADR-0003: pyramids-citymodels is a file-format driver package
  • ADR-0004: Versioned documentation strategy

Each ADR includes context, decision, and consequences. New ADRs should follow the numbering convention and be immutable once accepted.

docs.title: ADR-0001: Documentation stack
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text: We need a robust, contributor-friendly documentation stack that supports API reference, diagrams, tutorials, and versioned publishing — and that matches the rest of the stack, so a contributor moving between repositories does not relearn it.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Use MkDocs with the Material theme as the primary docs framework.
  • Use mkdocstrings[python] for auto-generating API reference from docstrings.
  • Prefer Mermaid fenced blocks for diagrams; allow PlantUML if complexity requires it.
  • Use mike to publish versioned documentation on GitHub Pages.
  • Execute example notebooks ahead of time and render their stored outputs (mkdocs-jupyter with execute: false); pixi run notebooks is what proves they still run.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Contributors document code with Google-style docstrings.
  • Diagrams render client-side in the site; heavy diagrams can be split or pre-rendered if needed.
  • CI builds the docs on pull requests, pushes to main, and releases, publishing with mike.

docs.title: ADR-0002: Type checking approach
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Static analysis improves reliability and developer experience, but the runtime stack underneath this package (GDAL via the vendored osgeo bindings, and the GIS types it extends) is only partially typed, so full strictness is not reachable from day one.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Adopt gradual typing with standard Python type hints; annotate public APIs first.
  • mypy is configured in [tool.mypy] (checker target 3.12, ignore_missing_imports for the untyped osgeo/pyramids-core surface, and lenient gradual-typing flags — disallow_untyped_defs = false, check_untyped_defs = true) and is enforced by the mypy pre-commit hook, which runs in CI (lint.yml). Contributors run it locally with pixi run -e dev mypy.
  • Prefer Google-style docstrings with type annotations to improve mkdocstrings output.
  • Geometry and feature arrays are annotated to match how pyramids annotates the same types, so signatures line up across the boundary.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Type hints are added progressively rather than in one sweep; the lenient flags keep the gate green while coverage grows, and strictness can be tightened per-module later without reworking existing annotations.
  • The checker target (3.12) is deliberately above the requires-python floor (3.11) so mypy can parse numpy's PEP 695 stubs; runtime 3.11 support is covered by the py311 test-matrix leg.

docs.title: ADR-0003: pyramids-citymodels is a file-format driver package
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
pyramids-core already ships the GIS data model — the raster Dataset, the vector FeatureCollection, the datacube — their GDAL/OGR-backed I/O, and every operation that follows once features are in hand: reprojection, overlays, spatial joins, filtering, geometry predicates, vector ↔ raster conversion and spatial indexing. This repository exists because the semantic 3D city-model exchange formats are missing from what the core opens, not because the GIS model needs a second implementation.

Without a stated boundary, the obvious failure mode is re-deriving geometry operations or re-wrapping the vector I/O here, which gives the stack two feature models that drift apart.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
pyramids-citymodels reads and writes the file formats of semantic 3D city models — CityGML, CityJSON and the related interchange formats — as pyramids objects. It owns file-format drivers; every GIS operation belongs upstream in pyramids-core.

  • Drivers are discovered by pyramids-core through the pyramids.vector_drivers entry-point group — the group pyramids.feature.FeatureCollection.read_file consults (siblings are pyramids.raster_drivers and pyramids.mesh_drivers). City models are vector features, so that is the group; pyramids has no city-model-specific consumer, and a driver registered under any other group would never be discovered. This package depends on pyramids-core; pyramids-core never imports this package.
  • Each driver is a VectorDriver class declaring name, long_name, api_version, suffixes, schemes, a capabilities set (containing read) and an optional extra, and implementing the can_open classmethod plus the read/write methods the format supports. pyramids reads those claims without constructing the driver and builds it only on a dispatched read, so a driver's heavy backend import belongs inside read, not at module top. When a driver's extra dependency is not importable the registry skips it silently at discovery (no warning), so a bare install stays small and useful.
  • Dependency-backed driver families live behind extras (one per family), added when the driver that needs one lands. Formats GDAL already reads (CityGML travels through GDAL's GML driver) use the vendored osgeo in the pyramids-core wheel rather than taking a new dependency.
  • Test fixtures are hand-built minimal files, committed, and kept out of the built distribution (setuptools' sdist does not collect tests/data/*, and the wheel is built from src/ only). Large vendor sample files are fetched in CI behind the vendor_data marker, never committed.

docs.title: The boundary
docs.text:
• pyramids-core remains the single owner of the GIS data model, its persistence, and every operation that follows from features already in hand. This package imports those types; it never redefines them.
  • Public functions take and return pyramids types, so a result can go straight back into the rest of the stack and be written through pyramids without a conversion step.
  • A gap or bug on the pyramids side of the boundary is reported and fixed upstream. A local workaround, if one is unavoidable, carries a comment naming the upstream issue and is removed when that lands.
  • Plotting goes through cleopatra, reached via pyramids. This package declares no plotting code and no plotting dependency: a driver returns data, and the caller plots it.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• The pyramids-core floor is an API floor on the driver registry, not on the GIS model. Raising it is the normal way to pick up an upstream fix the drivers depend on.
  • Semantic concerns a city-model format carries that pyramids-core does not yet model (rich LoD hierarchies, appearance/texture, semantic surfaces) are upstream work. A driver carries the value through without fabricating data rather than inventing a local model for it.
  • Interoperability is free — anything this package produces is already a pyramids object that the rest of the stack reads.

docs.title: ADR-0004: Versioned documentation strategy
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-10-25

docs.title: Context
docs.text: Readers need documentation matching the version they have installed, and contributors need to preview docs changes on a pull request before they merge.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• Use mike to publish versioned docs to GitHub Pages.
  • Track main as the development version; publish releases under their tag and alias latest.
  • Publish pull-request previews through the shared mkdocs-deploy action's pull_request trigger.
  • The release tag comes from pyproject.toml's version, which commitizen bumps — one source of truth for the package version, the git tag, and the docs version selector.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Contributors update docs alongside code and see a preview on the pull request.
  • Users browse historical docs aligned with releases.
  • A release that skips cz bump publishes docs under the wrong version, so version bumps stay commitizen-driven.

docs.title: Reading 3D city models¶
docs.text:
pyramids-citymodels reads CityJSON and CityGML LOD2 as pyramids features. The two formats are two serializations of one data model, so both parse into one shared representation and flatten into a FeatureCollection (a GeoDataFrame subclass) with one flat table: a surface_type column and a parent_id foreign key.

This notebook uses the driver classes directly. Once a released pyramids-core exposes the pyramids.vector_drivers registry, the same read runs through FeatureCollection.read_file(path, driver="cityjson") instead.

docs.title: CityJSON¶
docs.text: strategy="semantic_surfaces" (the default) gives one row per boundary surface, tagged with its surface_type. Coordinates keep their Z (2.5D).

docs.title: CityGML LOD2¶
docs.text: The CityGML reader reconstructs the same boundary-surface semantics from the GML, so the output table has the same shape as the CityJSON one.

docs.title: Footprints¶
docs.text: strategy="footprint" gives one 2D row per object — the plan-view union of its ground surfaces. Vertical walls are non-areal in plan view, so they are excluded from the footprint.

docs.title: Reference
docs.text:
The API surface of pyramids_citymodels, generated from the docstrings by mkdocstrings.

What this package publishes is drivers, not an API you call directly. A driver is a VectorDriver class registered with pyramids-core through the pyramids.vector_drivers entry-point group (the group FeatureCollection.read_file consults — city models are vector features), so installing this package is the whole integration: pyramids then dispatches a read of a city-model format it does not handle itself to the driver that claims it.

Each driver has its own page listing its suffixes, options and documented limitations:

Driver Format Page CityJsonDriver CityJSON Drivers CityGmlDriver CityGML LOD2 Drivers

See the Drivers page for the driver= / read_file usage and the read options, and the example notebook for a runnable walkthrough.

The package root deliberately re-exports nothing (__all__ is empty): it carries __version__ and the import contract that activates the vendored osgeo bindings. Driver classes are reached by their module path — pyramids_citymodels.drivers.<module>.<Driver> — which is also how their entry points name them, though normal use goes through pyramids rather than importing them at all.

For the GIS data model itself — the raster Dataset, the vector FeatureCollection, reprojection, overlays and conversion — see the pyramids reference. The split between the two is ADR-0003.

docs.title: pyramids_citymodels
docs.text:
3D city-model file-format drivers for the pyramids stack.

pyramids-citymodels reads and writes the file formats of semantic 3D city models — CityGML, CityJSON and the related interchange formats — as pyramids objects. pyramids-core owns the GIS data model (the raster Dataset, the vector FeatureCollection, the datacube), its GDAL/OGR-backed I/O, and every operation that follows once features are in hand — reprojection, overlays, spatial joins, conversion and spatial indexing. What it does not do is open the city-model exchange formats; that is this package's job, and its only job.

Drivers are discovered by pyramids-core through the pyramids.vector_drivers entry-point group (the group FeatureCollection.read_file consults — city models are vector features), so a read of a city-model file resolves to a driver here once this package is installed. A dependency-backed driver names its optional dependency via a VectorDriver.extra attribute and is skipped silently at discovery when that package is not importable. See ADR-0003 for the scope decision.

The package root deliberately re-exports nothing: it carries __version__ and the import contract that activates the vendored osgeo bindings, and that is all. Installing the package is the whole integration, so nothing here needs importing. A driver class is still reachable by its module path for the rare case of wanting one directly.

Examples:

  • The root carries the installed version and nothing else. __all__ is empty because there is deliberately nothing to re-export:

    import pyramids_citymodels pyramids_citymodels.version.split(".")[0].isdigit() True pyramids_citymodels.all []

docs.title: Drivers
docs.text:
pyramids-citymodels ships two readers for the 3D city-model exchange formats. Both turn a file into a pyramids FeatureCollection — a GeoDataFrame subclass — using one flat row model: a surface_type discriminator column and a parent_id foreign key, with the object's attributes passed through.

Driver name Formats (suffixes) Backend CityJsonDriver cityjson .city.json, .cityjson, .json (content-sniffed) stdlib json CityGmlDriver citygml .gml, .citygml, .xml (namespace-sniffed) stdlib xml.etree

Neither declares a separate GDAL or any heavy backend: parsing is pure standard library on top of the shapely/geopandas that pyramids-core already provides.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Once a released pyramids-core exposes the pyramids.vector_drivers registry, a city-model file is read through pyramids itself — the driver is selected by content, or named explicitly:

from pyramids.feature import FeatureCollection

# selected by content sniff (.json is shared with GeoJSON, so content decides)
features = FeatureCollection.read_file("building.city.json")
# or named explicitly
features = FeatureCollection.read_file("building.gml", driver="citygml")

Until that registry ships (tracked in #19), the drivers are used directly — the integration is otherwise identical:

from pyramids_citymodels.drivers.cityjson import CityJsonDriver

features = CityJsonDriver().read("building.city.json", strategy="semantic_surfaces")

docs.title: Read options
docs.text:
Both drivers' read forward the same keyword options to the flattener:

  • strategy — "semantic_surfaces" (default; one row per boundary surface) or "footprint" (one plan-view row per object).
  • lod — the level of detail to select; None (default) takes the highest each object offers.
  • geometry_dimension — "xyz" (default, keeps Z) or "xy" (drops Z). Ignored for a footprint.
  • child_inherits_parent_attributes — when True, a BuildingPart row also carries its Building's attributes.

A surface geometry is a planar polygon in 3D: a vertical wall is non-areal in the XY plane by design, so it is valid-but-zero-area in semantic_surfaces and excluded from a footprint. An unsupported geometry type (a point/line aggregate) raises UnsupportedGeometryError.

docs.title: pyramids_citymodels.drivers.cityjson
docs.text:
The CityJSON vector driver (issue #11).

Registered into the pyramids.vector_drivers entry-point group, this driver is what FeatureCollection.read_file dispatches a CityJSON read into. It follows the class-attribute contract pyramids' driver registry reads without constructing the driver: the claims (name/long_name/suffixes/…) are class attributes and :meth:can_open is a classmethod, so discovery never imports the parser or shapely/geopandas — those load only inside :meth:read, when a read is actually dispatched here.

The .json suffix is shared with GeoJSON, so a suffix alone cannot be trusted: :meth:can_open content-sniffs "type": "CityJSON" to claim a file, which cleanly separates CityJSON from a GeoJSON FeatureCollection (decision #3 in the ecosystem report).

docs.text:
Read CityJSON (.city.json / .json / .cityjson) as a FeatureCollection.

docs.title: pyramids_citymodels.readers.cityjson
docs.text:
Parse CityJSON into the shared IR (issue #6).

CityJSON stores every vertex once in a flat vertices array and encodes geometry boundaries as integer indices into it; coordinates are usually quantized integers that a transform (per-axis scale + translate) recovers to reals. Semantics are a parallel structure: a surfaces list of semantic objects plus a values index array that maps each boundary to one of them.

:func:parse_cityjson undoes all of that into the IR: it applies the transform, dereferences boundary indices to coordinate tuples (so downstream code never sees indices), carries the semantic surfaces/values through, and rebuilds the parent/child object hierarchy. It uses only the standard-library json module — no new dependency, matching what cjio, the QGIS Loader and plateaukit all do.

Versions 1.0, 1.1 and 2.0 share this layout; the version string is carried through on the model.

def parse_cityjson(source: Any) -> CityModel:
    """Parse a CityJSON document into a :class:`~pyramids_citymodels.ir.CityModel`.

    Args:
        source: A path to a ``.city.json``/``.json`` file, an open text file, a JSON string, or
            an already-decoded CityJSON ``dict``.

    Returns:
        The city model with every boundary dereferenced to transformed coordinate tuples.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the document is not a CityJSON object.

    Examples:
        - Parse an in-memory CityJSON document, then read its object and a transformed coordinate
          (the ``transform`` turns the quantized index ``1`` into the real point ``(1.0, 0.0, 0.0)``):
            ```python
            >>> doc = {
            ...     "type": "CityJSON", "version": "2.0",
            ...     "transform": {"scale": [0.001, 0.001, 0.001], "translate": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]},
            ...     "CityObjects": {"b": {"type": "Building", "geometry": [
            ...         {"type": "MultiSurface", "lod": "2", "boundaries": [[[0, 1, 2]]],
            ...          "semantics": {"surfaces": [{"type": "RoofSurface"}], "values": [0]}}]}},
            ...     "vertices": [[0, 0, 0], [1000, 0, 0], [1000, 1000, 0]]}
            >>> model = parse_cityjson(doc)
            >>> model.objects["b"].geometries[0].semantics[0].type
            'RoofSurface'
            >>> model.objects["b"].geometries[0].boundaries[0][0][1]
            (1.0, 0.0, 0.0)

            ```
    """
    document = _load(source)
    if not (isinstance(document, dict) and document.get("type") == "CityJSON"):
        raise ValueError("not a CityJSON document (missing 'type': 'CityJSON')")

    vertices = _transform_vertices(
        document.get("vertices", []), document.get("transform")
    )
    metadata = document.get("metadata", {}) or {}
    crs = crs_from_identifier(metadata.get("referenceSystem"))

    model = CityModel(
        crs=crs,
        metadata=metadata,
        version=str(document.get("version"))
        if document.get("version") is not None
        else None,
        source_format="CityJSON",
        # Carry the document-level appearance pool and any schema Extensions through untouched, so
        # materials/textures and third-party extensions are never silently dropped (#13).
        appearances=dict(document.get("appearance", {}) or {}),
        extensions=dict(document.get("extensions", {}) or {}),
    )

    for object_id, raw in document.get("CityObjects", {}).items():
        geometries = []
        for raw_geometry in raw.get("geometry", []):
            surfaces, values = _parse_semantics(raw_geometry.get("semantics"))
            lod = raw_geometry.get("lod")
            appearance = {
                key: raw_geometry[key]
                for key in ("material", "texture")
                if key in raw_geometry
            }
            geometries.append(
                Geometry(
                    type=raw_geometry.get("type", "Unknown"),
                    lod=None if lod is None else str(lod),
                    boundaries=_dereference(
                        raw_geometry.get("boundaries", []), vertices
                    ),
                    semantics=surfaces,
                    semantic_values=values,
                    appearance=appearance or None,
                )
            )
        model.objects[object_id] = CityObject(
            id=object_id,
            type=raw.get("type", "Unknown"),
            attributes=dict(raw.get("attributes", {}) or {}),
            geometries=geometries,
            parents=list(raw.get("parents", []) or []),
            children=list(raw.get("children", []) or []),
        )

    return model

def looks_like_cityjson(source: Any) -> bool:
    """Return ``True`` when ``source`` is a CityJSON document (``"type": "CityJSON"``).

    This is the content sniff the driver's ``can_open`` uses to tell CityJSON from GeoJSON for a
    bare ``.json`` file: a GeoJSON ``FeatureCollection`` has ``"type": "FeatureCollection"``, a
    CityJSON file has ``"type": "CityJSON"``. Reading is cheap and never raises — a file that is
    not JSON, or not a JSON object, simply returns ``False``.

    Examples:
        - A CityJSON document is recognized, a GeoJSON one sharing the suffix is not:
            ```python
            >>> doc = '{"type": "CityJSON", "version": "2.0", "CityObjects": {}, "vertices": []}'
            >>> looks_like_cityjson(doc)
            True
            >>> looks_like_cityjson('{"type": "FeatureCollection", "features": []}')
            False

            ```
        - Content that is not JSON at all is declined without raising:
            ```python
            >>> looks_like_cityjson("not json at all")
            False

            ```
    """
    try:
        document = _load(source)
    except (OSError, ValueError, TypeError):
        return False
    return isinstance(document, dict) and document.get("type") == "CityJSON"

docs.text:
Parse CityGML LOD2 semantic buildings into the shared IR (issue #7).

CityGML is schema-heavy GML/XML: a bldg:Building has optional bldg:BuildingPart children, each carrying boundary surfaces (WallSurface, RoofSurface, GroundSurface, …) that in turn carry gml:Polygon rings. This reader reconstructs that LOD2 semantic model — Building → BuildingPart → boundary surface → polygon — because the raw geometry is already reachable through GDAL's GML driver; the semantics are what is missing (issue #1384).

It parses with the standard-library xml.etree.ElementTree (no lxml, no new dependency) and matches elements by local name, ignoring the namespace, so one code path handles CityGML 1.0 (.../1.0), 2.0 (.../2.0) and 3.0 (.../3.0) rather than hardcoding a version's namespace URIs. A building (or part) becomes one :class:~pyramids_citymodels.ir.Geometry of type "MultiSurface" whose surfaces are its boundary polygons, each tagged with the local name of its boundary-surface element as the semantic type. A BuildingPart becomes its own city object, linked to its parent building.

    Note:
        Shared geometry (``xlink:href``) is resolved against a document-wide ``gml:id`` index, so a
        polygon referenced by href is attributed to **every** referencing feature (legitimate CityGML
        shared geometry). Within one feature a polygon reachable from two boundary surfaces is taken
        **once**, keeping the first (document-order) surface's semantic type.

    Examples:
        - Parse an in-memory CityGML building and read its reconstructed semantic surface:
            ```python
            >>> xml = '''<core:CityModel
            ...   xmlns:core="http://www.opengis.net/citygml/2.0"
            ...   xmlns:bldg="http://www.opengis.net/citygml/building/2.0"
            ...   xmlns:gml="http://www.opengis.net/gml">
            ...   <core:cityObjectMember><bldg:Building gml:id="B">
            ...     <bldg:boundedBy><bldg:RoofSurface>
            ...       <bldg:lod2MultiSurface><gml:MultiSurface><gml:surfaceMember>
            ...         <gml:Polygon><gml:exterior><gml:LinearRing>
            ...           <gml:posList srsDimension="3">0 0 1 1 0 1 1 1 1</gml:posList>
            ...         </gml:LinearRing></gml:exterior></gml:Polygon>
            ...       </gml:surfaceMember></gml:MultiSurface></bldg:lod2MultiSurface>
            ...     </bldg:RoofSurface></bldg:boundedBy>
            ...   </bldg:Building></core:cityObjectMember>
            ... </core:CityModel>'''
            >>> model = parse_citygml(xml)
            >>> model.objects["B"].geometries[0].semantics[0].type
            'RoofSurface'

            ```
    """
    root = _read_tree(source)
    parent_of = {child: parent for parent in root.iter() for child in parent}

    # CRS: the first srsName seen anywhere (envelope or geometry).
    crs = None
    for element in root.iter():
        for key, value in element.attrib.items():
            if _local(key) == "srsName":
                crs = crs_from_identifier(value)
                break
        if crs:
            break

    default_dimension = 3

    # Assign a stable id to every Building / BuildingPart up front, so boundary surfaces can be
    # attributed to the nearest one by walking ancestors.
    feature_ids: dict[ElementTree.Element, str] = {}
    anonymous = 0
    for element in root.iter():
        if _local(element.tag) in ("Building", "BuildingPart"):
            identifier = _gml_id(element)
            if not identifier:
                identifier = f"{_local(element.tag)}_{anonymous}"
                anonymous += 1
            feature_ids[element] = identifier

    model = CityModel(crs=crs, source_format="CityGML", version=_detect_version(root))

    # Create a city object per feature, with parent/child links between a part and its building.
    for element, identifier in feature_ids.items():
        parent_feature_id = _nearest_feature_id(element, parent_of, feature_ids)
        city_object = CityObject(
            id=identifier,
            type=_local(element.tag),
            attributes=_collect_building_attributes(element),
            parents=[parent_feature_id] if parent_feature_id else [],
        )
        model.objects[identifier] = city_object
        if parent_feature_id:
            model.objects[parent_feature_id].children.append(identifier)

    # Index every polygon by its gml:id so a boundary surface that references its geometry by
    # xlink:href (shared-geometry / XLink graph) can resolve it instead of silently dropping it.
    polygons_by_id: dict[str, ElementTree.Element] = {}
    for node in root.iter():
        if _local(node.tag) == "Polygon":
            polygon_id = _gml_id(node)
            if polygon_id:
                polygons_by_id[polygon_id] = node

    # Gather boundary surfaces, attributing each to its nearest feature and tagging its semantics.
    surfaces_by_feature: dict[
        str, tuple[list[Any], list[SemanticSurface], list[int]]
    ] = {identifier: ([], [], []) for identifier in feature_ids.values()}
    # One polygon reachable from two boundary surfaces of a feature (inline in one, referenced by
    # xlink:href from another) must be collected ONCE, keeping the first (document-order) surface's
    # semantic type — so the seen-set is scoped to the feature, not reset per boundary surface (SF1).
    seen_by_feature: dict[str, set[int]] = {
        identifier: set() for identifier in feature_ids.values()
    }
    for element in root.iter():
        local = _local(element.tag)
        if local not in _BOUNDARY_SURFACE_NAMES:
            continue
        feature_id = _nearest_feature_id(element, parent_of, feature_ids)
        if feature_id is None:
            continue
        boundaries, semantics, values = surfaces_by_feature[feature_id]
        seen = seen_by_feature[feature_id]
        for node in element.iter():
            polygon: ElementTree.Element | None = None
            if _local(node.tag) == "Polygon":
                polygon = node
            else:
                referenced = _href(node)
                if referenced:
                    polygon = polygons_by_id.get(referenced)
            if polygon is None or id(polygon) in seen:
                continue
            seen.add(id(polygon))
            surface = _surfaces_from_polygon(polygon, default_dimension)
            if not surface or len(surface[0]) < 3:
                continue
            values.append(len(semantics))
            semantics.append(SemanticSurface(type=local))
            boundaries.append(surface)

    for identifier, (boundaries, semantics, values) in surfaces_by_feature.items():
        if boundaries:
            model.objects[identifier].geometries.append(
                Geometry(
                    type="MultiSurface",
                    lod="2",
                    boundaries=boundaries,
                    semantics=semantics,
                    semantic_values=values,
                )
            )

    return model

def looks_like_citygml(source: Any) -> bool:
    """Return ``True`` when ``source`` is a CityGML document.

    Sniffs the XML for a CityGML namespace or a ``CityModel`` / ``cityObjectMember`` element, so
    the driver's ``can_open`` claims real CityGML and declines a plain GML or arbitrary XML file.
    Never raises — a non-XML or unreadable file returns ``False``.

    Examples:
        - A CityGML-namespaced document is recognized; plain XML is declined:
            ```python
            >>> looks_like_citygml('<core:CityModel xmlns:core="http://www.opengis.net/citygml/2.0"/>')
            True
            >>> looks_like_citygml("<root><child/></root>")
            False

            ```
    """
    try:
        for _event, element in _iterparse_start(source, limit=200):
            tag = _local(element.tag)
            # ``CityModel`` / ``cityObjectMember`` are CityGML-specific element names; ``Building``
            # is deliberately NOT a marker, because a plain (non-CityGML) GML feature collection can
            # carry a ``Building`` and must not be hijacked from OGR (SF2). A ``bldg``-namespaced
            # Building is still recognized below, since its namespace contains ``citygml``.
            if tag in ("CityModel", "cityObjectMember"):
                return True
            namespace = (
                element.tag[1:].split("}", 1)[0] if element.tag.startswith("{") else ""
            )
            if "citygml" in namespace.lower():
                return True
    except (OSError, ElementTree.ParseError, TypeError, ValueError):
        return False
    return False

docs.text:
Flatten the IR into a FeatureCollection row model (issue #8).

The 3D, hierarchical city model becomes a flat feature table using the pattern 3DCityDB and the QGIS Loader both converge on: one flat table, a surface_type discriminator column and a parent_id foreign key, with object attributes passed through. That single shape serves both load strategies (:class:~pyramids_citymodels.options.LoadStrategy):

  • semantic_surfaces — one row per boundary surface, carrying surface_type (RoofSurface, WallSurface, …), the owning object's id/type, its parent_id and its attributes.
  • footprint — one row per city object, geometry = the 2D union of its ground surfaces (or, when a model tags no ground, the 2D union of all its surfaces).

Z is kept or dropped per :class:~pyramids_citymodels.options.GeometryDimension (a footprint is always 2D). Identical polygons within one object are de-duplicated, which collapses the common XLink case where one polygon is referenced by both a semantic surface and a solid shell.

Surface geometries are planar polygons in 3D (2.5D). A building's vertical surface — a wall — is a real polygon in 3D space whose projection onto the XY plane is a straight line. Shapely measures validity and area on that XY footprint only, so a wall row is deliberately non-areal: is_valid is False and area is 0 for it, while roofs and ground (near-horizontal) are valid with positive area. This is the documented semantic_surfaces contract, not a defect — operate on the surfaces in 3D (the Z is preserved in xyz mode), and treat 2D-areal operations (overlay, area, to_file of a 2D driver) as meaningful only for the horizontal surfaces or for a footprint load. The footprint load, being a plan projection, excludes these non-areal surfaces.

The result is a :class:pyramids.feature.FeatureCollection — a GeoDataFrame subclass — so it flows straight into the rest of the pyramids stack; this module builds no GIS of its own.

def to_feature_collection(
    model: CityModel,
    *,
    strategy: "str | LoadStrategy" = LoadStrategy.SEMANTIC_SURFACES,
    lod: Any = None,
    geometry_dimension: "str | GeometryDimension" = GeometryDimension.XYZ,
    child_inherits_parent_attributes: bool = False,
) -> FeatureCollection:
    """Flatten a :class:`~pyramids_citymodels.ir.CityModel` into a ``FeatureCollection``.

    Args:
        model: The parsed city model.
        strategy: ``"footprint"`` (one row per object) or ``"semantic_surfaces"`` (one row per
            boundary surface). Accepts a :class:`~pyramids_citymodels.options.LoadStrategy`.
        lod: Level of detail to select; ``None`` takes the highest each object offers. An explicit
            ``lod`` that no object carries selects nothing and yields an **empty** FeatureCollection
            (no error) — pass ``None`` to always get the best available.
        geometry_dimension: ``"xyz"`` keeps Z, ``"xy"`` drops it. Ignored for ``footprint``.
        child_inherits_parent_attributes: When ``True``, child rows also carry parent attributes.

    Note:
        The structural columns ``city_object_id``, ``city_object_type``, ``parent_id``, ``lod``,
        ``surface_type`` and ``surface_index`` take precedence: a city-object attribute that happens
        to share one of these names is overwritten by the structural value in the output table.

        A ``footprint`` load omits an object whose surfaces are **all non-areal** (e.g. a wall-only
        object): it has no plan-view area, so it contributes no row. This is omission by design, not
        data loss — use ``semantic_surfaces`` to keep every surface.

    Returns:
        A :class:`pyramids.feature.FeatureCollection` in the model's CRS, with a stable column
        order; empty (but still a valid FeatureCollection) when the model has no usable geometry.

    Examples:
        - Flatten a one-building model into one row per semantic surface and read it back:
            ```python
            >>> from pyramids_citymodels.readers.cityjson import parse_cityjson
            >>> doc = {
            ...     "type": "CityJSON", "version": "2.0",
            ...     "CityObjects": {"b": {"type": "Building", "geometry": [
            ...         {"type": "MultiSurface", "lod": "2", "boundaries": [[[0, 1, 2]]],
            ...          "semantics": {"surfaces": [{"type": "RoofSurface"}], "values": [0]}}]}},
            ...     "vertices": [[0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0], [1, 1, 0]]}
            >>> frame = to_feature_collection(parse_cityjson(doc), strategy="semantic_surfaces")
            >>> len(frame)
            1
            >>> frame["surface_type"].iloc[0]
            'RoofSurface'

            ```
    """
    options = ReadOptions.coerce(
        strategy=strategy,
        lod=lod,
        geometry_dimension=geometry_dimension,
        child_inherits_parent_attributes=child_inherits_parent_attributes,
    )

    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for city_object in model.objects.values():
        geometries = _select_geometries(city_object.geometries, options.lod)
        if not geometries:
            continue
        for geometry in geometries:
            if geometry.type not in AREAL_GEOMETRY_TYPES:
                raise UnsupportedGeometryError(
                    f"city object {city_object.id!r} has geometry type {geometry.type!r}, "
                    f"which is not areal; supported types are "
                    f"{', '.join(sorted(AREAL_GEOMETRY_TYPES))}"
                )
        if options.strategy is LoadStrategy.SEMANTIC_SURFACES:
            rows.extend(_semantic_surface_rows(city_object, geometries, model, options))
        else:
            row = _footprint_row(city_object, geometries, model, options)
            if row is not None:
                rows.append(row)

    if rows:
        frame = gpd.GeoDataFrame(rows, geometry="geometry", crs=model.crs)
    else:
        frame = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"geometry": []}, geometry="geometry", crs=model.crs)
    return FeatureCollection(frame)

docs.text:
Read options: how the 3D, hierarchical city model is projected onto flat features.

A GeoDataFrame is 2D-centric, flat and one-geometry-per-row; a city model is 3D, hierarchical and graph-linked. There is no single right projection, so the projection is exposed as options rather than hardcoded — the lesson the QGIS CityJSON Loader and 3DCityDB both teach (issues #9 and #10):

  • :class:LoadStrategy — what a row is: one row per city object (its footprint) or one row per semantic surface (wall/roof/ground as individual features).
  • :class:GeometryDimension — how Z is carried: dropped for a 2D footprint, or kept for 2.5D surfaces. A footprint load is always 2D regardless, since a footprint is a plan projection.
  • lod — which level of detail to select when a city object carries several.
  • child_inherits_parent_attributes — whether a BuildingPart row also carries its Building's attributes.

:class:ReadOptions bundles these, and :meth:ReadOptions.coerce accepts either the enums or their plain-string values so a driver can pass user kwargs straight through.

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class ReadOptions:
    """The resolved set of read options the flattener consumes.

    Attributes:
        strategy: The :class:`LoadStrategy`.
        lod: The level of detail to select, or ``None`` to take the highest each object offers.
        geometry_dimension: The :class:`GeometryDimension` (ignored for a footprint load, which
            is always 2D).
        child_inherits_parent_attributes: When ``True``, a child object's rows also carry its
            parent's attributes (the parent's values do not overwrite the child's own).
    """

    strategy: LoadStrategy = LoadStrategy.SEMANTIC_SURFACES
    lod: str | None = None
    geometry_dimension: GeometryDimension = GeometryDimension.XYZ
    child_inherits_parent_attributes: bool = False

    @classmethod
    def coerce(
        cls,
        strategy: "str | LoadStrategy" = LoadStrategy.SEMANTIC_SURFACES,
        lod: Any = None,
        geometry_dimension: "str | GeometryDimension" = GeometryDimension.XYZ,
        child_inherits_parent_attributes: bool = False,
    ) -> "ReadOptions":
        """Build a :class:`ReadOptions`, accepting enums or their plain-string values.

        Raises:
            ValueError: If ``strategy`` or ``geometry_dimension`` is not a recognized value.

        Examples:
            >>> ReadOptions.coerce(strategy="footprint").strategy is LoadStrategy.FOOTPRINT
            True
            >>> ReadOptions.coerce(geometry_dimension="xy").geometry_dimension
            <GeometryDimension.XY: 'xy'>
            >>> ReadOptions.coerce(lod=2).lod
            '2'
        """
        try:
            resolved_strategy = LoadStrategy(strategy)
        except ValueError as error:
            valid = ", ".join(repr(member.value) for member in LoadStrategy)
            raise ValueError(
                f"unknown strategy {strategy!r}; expected one of {valid}"
            ) from error
        try:
            resolved_dimension = GeometryDimension(geometry_dimension)
        except ValueError as error:
            valid = ", ".join(repr(member.value) for member in GeometryDimension)
            raise ValueError(
                f"unknown geometry_dimension {geometry_dimension!r}; expected one of {valid}"
            ) from error
        return cls(
            strategy=resolved_strategy,
            lod=None if lod is None else str(lod),
            geometry_dimension=resolved_dimension,
            child_inherits_parent_attributes=bool(child_inherits_parent_attributes),
        )

class UnsupportedGeometryError(CityModelError):
    """A geometry whose type cannot be represented as areal features.

    Raised when the flattener meets a geometry type it does not map to polygons — a point or line
    aggregate (``MultiPoint``, ``MultiLineString``) or a template reference (``GeometryInstance``).
    Rejecting these explicitly, with the offending object id and type, is deliberate: silently
    dropping them would hand back an empty row set with no indication why (report §5, risk #8).
    """
